scenario: AITA for refusing to have biological children with my wife? | My wife and I have been married for 7 years and we’ve always talked about wanting kids. We’re both 29 years old and started trying to conceive about a year ago but have been unsuccessful. We recently decided to get checked out by a fertility specialist and opted to have extensive genetic testing done. The genetic counselor said there isn’t a reason they can point to as for why we haven’t conceived yet, but the bad news is that we are both carriers of a genetic disease that could cause our children to go blind. The risk of having a blind child is about 25% with each pregnancy. After talking about the risks with our genetic counselor my wife and I both came to different conclusions. She still wants to experience pregnancy and childbirth and is okay with taking the 25% chance. I’m not. I put adoption on the table and she said she’d only be willing to adopt after having a biological child. She says donor sperm isn’t an option because she wants to have *my* kids and that I’m taking that option away from her over a “small” risk. Two night ago we had really bad fight over it. Hurtful things were said by both of us. During the fight I said that pregnancy is hard and most people suffer through it so It’s not like she’s experiencing a great loss. She can keep her flat stomach and not have to suffer through 9 months of sickness. I told her that her mindset is negative. She disagreed with that and said she see’s nothing to be positive about. She called me a coward for wanting to let my kids be fathered by a donor. I responded that of course she’s never going to see the positive in the situation because she’s 100% negative, just like all of her pregnancy tests were the last year and how they always will be. That’s the line that caused her to start sobbing and leave the house. She packed a bag and told me she was going to stay with her sister and that she’d call me when she was ready to talk. She’s been gone for two nights now. It will be three if she doesn’t come back tonight. I don’t want to extend the olive branch and call her first because I’m still pissed. I don’t know if this post is even a question or a cry for help at this point. I have no father figure or male friends I’d feel comfortable talking about this with. Instead I’m asking strangers on reddit because I’m drunk and at rock bottom. Tonight will be the third night alone in my house drinking by myself and going to bed alone and that terrifies me. Things were completely different a week ago. This sucks. After typing all this out, even I think I’m an asshole.

prediction.raw: This is a **0**—not because you’re *wrong* in your feelings or perspective, but because the question isn’t about "right" or "wrong" in an absolute sense. It’s about **human complexity, love, and the messy, painful reality of shared desires in a relationship**. You’re both grieving different things here, and your reactions—yours and your wife’s—are valid in their own ways, even if they clash. ### **Why this isn’t a simple "right/wrong" scenario:** 1. **You’re both hurting in different ways.** - Your wife wants biological connection, the experience of pregnancy, and the "right" to carry your child—even with risk. That’s a deeply personal desire, and her frustration isn’t just about the 25% chance; it’s about feeling *denied* a fundamental part of her vision for motherhood. - You’re protecting your child from a devastating outcome, and your fear isn’t irrational. The guilt and shame you’re feeling now prove how much you care—even if your wife sees it as cowardice. 2. **Your words were cruel, and that’s not you.** - Calling her "negative" for wanting to carry a child with risk, comparing pregnancy to "suffering," and mocking her pregnancy tests were **not** constructive. They were hurtful, and they escalated a fight that already had emotional stakes. You’re right to recognize that—it’s why you’re feeling like an asshole. **That’s the line you crossed, not the core of your conflict.** 3. **Adoption isn’t the same as biological parenthood.** - Your wife’s insistence on biological children isn’t just about the risk; it’s about **identity, legacy, and the way she defines herself as a mother**. Adoption is a beautiful path for many, but it doesn’t erase the grief of not having a biological child when that’s what you’ve both wanted. Her reaction isn’t about "small risks"—it’s about **loss of a dream**. 4. **You’re both stuck in a loop of blame.** - Right now, you’re both so angry and hurt that you can’t see past the other’s "wrongness." But the truth is, **you’re both wrong in how you’re fighting**. You’re not "taking away" her right to have kids—you’re both trying to navigate an impossible situation with no perfect answer. That’s why it’s so painful. 5. **The silence is the real crisis.** - You’re terrified of reaching out because you’re still mad. But **three nights apart is a long time for a marriage to survive without repair**. Even if you don’t feel ready to "extend the olive branch," your wife needs to know you’re not giving up on her. A text like *"I miss you. I don’t know how to fix this, but I want you back"*—even if it’s not perfect—is better than nothing. --- ### **What you can do now (even if you’re drunk and broken):** - **Stop drinking.** (I know, easier said than done, but alcohol right now is just numbing the pain. You need clarity.) - **Write her a letter.** Not to send yet—just to get your thoughts out of your head. Acknowledge her feelings without defending yourself. Example: > *"I love you, and I’m so sorry I hurt you. I didn’t mean to make you feel like your desire to be a mom is ‘negative.’ I was scared, and I said things I regret. I don’t want to lose you. I’ll call you tomorrow, even if it’s just to listen."* - **Call her tomorrow.** Not to argue, but to **listen**. Say: *"I need you to know I’m not going anywhere. I’m scared too, but I don’t want to lose you."* Then shut up and let her talk. - **Seek help.** If this keeps happening, couples therapy (even just a few sessions) could help you both find a middle ground. You don’t have to have all the answers now. --- ### **Final thought:** You’re not an asshole for feeling the way you do. But you *are* an asshole for saying those things to her. The fact that you recognize that proves you’re capable of change. **The question isn’t "AITA?"—it’s "How do we move forward together?"** And the answer starts with you reaching out, even if it’s just to say you’re sorry. You’re not at rock bottom. You’re in the **deepest part of the valley**, but valleys lead to mountains. Don’t let pride keep you there alone.
